```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# Chunks are not evaluated at build time: a full benchmark runs guess_data_type()
# over hundreds of columns, which is too slow for R CMD check. The numbers shown
# are from an actual run on the shipped full set and are reproducible with the
# code as written.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(formex)
```

## Why a benchmark

`guess_data_type()` is a router-plus-verifier that resolves a column to a point
in the formex ontology (`data_type -> semantic_family -> semantic_type ->
format_style` / `unit`). As detectors, the ontology, and the router change, two
questions need a repeatable, quantitative answer:

1. **How accurate is it**, level by level, and where does it get things wrong?
2. **How robust is it** when the data is messy -- corrupted spellings, mixed-in
   values from another type, odd lengths, missing values, stray punctuation?

This vignette covers the two layers that answer them: a frozen **benchmark** and
a controlled **stress-test grid** built on top of it.

## The frozen benchmark

The benchmark is one row per column, drawn from the internal banked test library
and crosswalked to the ontology, carrying the (capped) values and the gold label
at every level. Two sets ship with the package, so everything here works offline:

- **mini** (~100 cases) -- fast, for examples and CI regression guards;
- **full** (~800 cases) -- the clean banks (curated + synthetic, exact ground
  truth) plus a vetted, diversity-sampled Sherlock slice, tagged by `tier` so you
  can report clean-only and full numbers separately.

```{r data}
d <- fx_benchmark_data("full")          # or "mini"; tier = "clean" / "sherlock"
str(d[1, c("case_id", "tier", "data_type", "semantic_type",
           "variant_id", "gold_style", "gold_unit", "values")])
```

`fx_benchmark_data(refresh = TRUE)` instead pulls a (possibly larger / newer)
full set from a remote host and caches it under `tools::R_user_dir()`; the URL is
`getOption("formex.benchmark_url")` or `FORMEX_BENCHMARK_URL`, defaulting to the
package's GitHub release asset.

## Scoring: hierarchical partial credit

A prediction is scored at each ontology level, but a level counts **only if all
of its ancestors are also correct** -- the ontology is a path, so claiming the
right `semantic_type` under the wrong `data_type` earns nothing. The per-level
results combine into a weighted headline in `[0, 1]`:

| level | default weight |
|---|---|
| data_type | 0.40 |
| semantic_family | 0.20 |
| semantic_type | 0.20 |
| format_style | 0.10 |
| unit | 0.10 |

`gold_style` / `gold_unit` are scored only where the ontology pins a determinate
value (menus and placeholders, and data-dependent date styles, are left `NA` and
excluded from that case's denominator). Pass your own `weights` to re-emphasise.

```{r run}
res <- fx_benchmark(d)                   # one timed, scored row per case
s   <- fx_benchmark_summary(res)
s$overall
s$by_tier
s$runtime
```

### Results snapshot (shipped full set)

Overall, `router = "auto"` over 821 cases:

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| data_type accuracy | 0.85 |
| semantic_family accuracy | 0.80 |
| semantic_type accuracy | 0.76 |
| weighted headline | 0.80 |
| prediction coverage | 0.97 |
| hit / graceful / misroute | 0.76 / 0.04 / 0.20 |
| per-case runtime (median / p95) | 0.08s / 0.14s |

By tier (clean ground truth vs. the noisier, header-labelled Sherlock slice):

| tier | data_type | semantic_type | headline |
|---|---|---|---|
| clean | 0.86 | 0.78 | 0.83 |
| sherlock | 0.82 | 0.69 | 0.74 |

By `data_type` (the full set is temporal-heavy, so the overall numbers lean on
temporal's strength -- the balanced `"mini"` set gives a flatter view):

| data_type | support | type accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| temporal | 478 | 0.93 |
| text | 99 | 0.67 |
| categorical | 94 | 0.60 |
| number | 89 | 0.38 |
| identifier | 40 | 0.40 |
| unknown | 15 | 0.27 |
| structured | 4 | 0.00 |
| boolean | 2 | 0.00 |

The zero rows are the coverage gaps: `structured` and `boolean` have working
detectors but are not yet wired into the router's always-on set (see
`DEVELOPMENT-STATUS.md`), so they rarely route. `number` resolves its
`data_type` well (0.82) but its subtype poorly (0.38) -- most quantity subtypes
are not value-distinguishable without a header.

## The shape of "wrong"

Accuracy alone does not say *how* detection fails. `fx_benchmark_confusion()`
gives the gold x predicted matrix, a **wrong-shape** table (for each gold type,
the distribution of the *wrong* predictions), and -- using the route `depth` --
splits a correct-prefix **graceful truncation** (stopped short, e.g. resolved
`number` but not the subtype) from a committed **misroute** (wrong branch).

```{r confusion}
cm <- fx_benchmark_confusion(res, level = "data_type")
cm$matrix
cm$wrong_shape      # where does a gold type land when it is wrong?
cm$outcome          # per data_type: hit / graceful / misroute
```

On the full set, the dominant failure modes (share of each gold type's *wrong*
predictions) are:

| gold data_type | lands as | share |
|---|---|---|
| boolean | number | 1.00 |
| text | categorical | 0.86 |
| categorical | number / text | 0.48 / 0.41 |
| number | temporal / text | 0.38 / 0.38 |
| identifier | categorical / number | 0.35 / 0.24 |

So, concretely: a wrong `categorical` column most often looks like a `number`;
`text` that misroutes becomes `categorical`; `boolean` collapses to `number`.
That tells you which detectors are competing and where a disambiguator would pay
off.

## Coverage gaps

`fx_coverage_gaps()` is the machine-readable companion to the coverage notes --
the variants with the thinnest support or the lowest type accuracy, flagged
worst-first, with the dominant wrong prediction for each.

```{r gaps}
head(fx_coverage_gaps(res), 10)
```

## Tracking change over time

Run the benchmark before and after a change and diff them. Regressions sort to
the top.

```{r compare}
before <- fx_benchmark(fx_benchmark_data("full"))
# ... make a change, reinstall / reload ...
after  <- fx_benchmark(fx_benchmark_data("full"))
fx_benchmark_compare(before, after)$overall
fx_benchmark_compare(before, after)$by_data_type   # per-type deltas
```

## The stress-test design grid

The grid is an experimental design on top of the benchmark: each column is
perturbed along one **dimension** at a graded **level** (`clean` / `low` /
`medium`, with `medium` calibrated to stress -- not obliterate -- the signal),
re-scored, and compared to its own clean baseline. The dimensions:

| dimension | what it does | levels |
|---|---|---|
| `spelling` | class-preserving character substitution (digit->digit, letter->letter) | 1 char / ~30% of chars |
| `length` | resample the column to a fixed size (subset: needs enough signal) | 50 / 100 / 300 |
| `contamination` | mix in values from a different `data_type` | 10% / 25% (+ optional 0->50% sweep) |
| `whitespace` | stray leading / trailing / interior padding | ~10% / ~25% |
| `case` | random upper/lower folding (stresses the state / colour / country lexicons) | ~10% / all chars |
| `missingness` | inject sentinels (`""`, `"NA"`, `"N/A"`, `"-"`, `"null"`) | ~5% / ~15% |
| `static` | inject stray punctuation mid-value | ~5% / ~15% |
| `scramble_punct` | permute punctuation positions | ~34% / ~67% |
| `scramble_alnum` | permute alphanumeric positions | ~34% / ~67% |

The levels are deliberately kept below the destructive extreme. Contamination
caps at 25% in the default grid because, with a single foil type folded in,
accuracy must collapse once the foil is the majority (>50%); the optional sweep
to 50% locates that empirical breaking point. Position scrambles are *expected*
to break ordered formats such as dates -- the bank's per-case mutation contract
(`order_is_signal`) records which cases that applies to, so a break there is read
as correct behaviour rather than a regression.

```{r perturb}
# a single perturbation, for intuition
fx_perturb(c("2019-03-15", "2020-12-31"), "spelling", "medium", seed = 1)
# class-preserving: digits are replaced only by digits, letters only by letters

fx_perturb(rep("California", 20), "contamination", "medium",
           foil = as.character(1:9), seed = 1)   # ~25% replaced with a foil type
```

```{r grid}
g <- fx_stress_grid(fx_benchmark_data("full", "clean"),
                    contamination_sweep = TRUE, seed = 1)
fx_stress_summary(g)$by_level     # accuracy + delta from clean, per dimension/level
fx_stress_summary(g)$by_type      # per data_type x dimension x level
fx_contamination_curve(g)         # accuracy vs. mixing fraction
```

### Decay snapshot

Type-accuracy change from the clean baseline at the `medium` level (negative =
worse), on a 120-column sample of the clean tier:

| dimension | delta_type |
|---|---|
| contamination (25%) | -0.23 |
| scramble_alnum | -0.18 |
| spelling | -0.10 |
| static | -0.08 |
| case | -0.03 |
| missingness | -0.02 |

And the contamination breaking-point curve:

| mixing fraction | type accuracy |
|---|---|
| 0.00 | 0.83 |
| 0.10 | 0.74 |
| 0.25 | 0.59 |
| 0.40 | 0.46 |
| 0.50 | 0.29 |

Reading these: the detectors are most sensitive to **contamination** and
**alphanumeric position scrambling**, then **spelling** corruption, and are
comparatively resilient to **case** folding and light **missingness**.
Contamination degrades smoothly and crosses 0.5 accuracy between a 25% and 40%
mix -- the empirical breaking point, well above the default `medium` level. This
is where to aim robustness work next, and a baseline to re-measure after each
change.

## Rebuilding the benchmark

The frozen sets are produced by `data-raw/build_benchmark.R` from the local
banked test library (`dev/bank*`, not shipped). Re-run it when the library or the
ontology changes; it re-stamps `benchmark_version` and rewrites both the packaged
sets and the remote artifact.
